name: Natural numbers
definition: The counting numbers 1, 2, 3, … (some authors include 0; check the local convention). They support induction: prove a base case and the step from n to n+1.

examples.explanation: n is a natural number.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Integers
definition: All whole numbers, positive, negative and zero: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …. The symbol comes from German “Zahlen” (numbers).

examples.explanation: Negative three is an integer.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Rational numbers
definition: All ratios of integers with nonzero denominator. Decimals of rationals always terminate or repeat; anything else is irrational.

examples.explanation: Two thirds is rational.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Real numbers
definition: All rationals plus irrationals: every point on the number line. The reals are complete, meaning limits of convergent sequences stay inside.

examples.explanation: Root two is real but not rational.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Complex numbers
definition: Numbers a + bi with real a, b and i² = −1. Every nonzero complex number has a magnitude and an angle; every polynomial equation has a complex root (fundamental theorem of algebra).

examples.explanation: Real part 3, imaginary part 4.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Imaginary unit
definition: The number with i² = −1, extending the reals to the complex plane. Engineers often write j instead, since i means current.

examples.explanation: Powers of i cycle every four.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Complex conjugate
definition: Reflects a complex number across the real axis by negating its imaginary part. A number times its conjugate gives its squared magnitude.

examples.explanation: Flip the sign of the imaginary part.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Real and imaginary parts
definition: Extract the components of z = a + bi: Re(z) = a and Im(z) = b. Note Im(z) is the real number b, not bi.
reading: “the real part of z” and “the imaginary part of z”.

examples.explanation: Components of 3 + 4i.

commonMistakes: Writing Im(3+4i) = 4i; the imaginary part is the real coefficient 4.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Complex modulus
definition: The distance of z from the origin: |a + bi| = √(a² + b²). It generalizes absolute value to the complex plane and equals √(z·z̄).

examples.explanation: A 3-4-5 triangle from the origin.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Euler's identity
definition: Links five fundamental constants in one equation. It is the special case x = π of Euler's formula e^(ix) = cos x + i·sin x.
reading: “e to the i pi plus one equals zero”.

examples.explanation: Euler's formula: rotation in the complex plane.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 4
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Gamma function
definition: Extends the factorial to non-integers: Γ(n) = (n−1)! for positive integers, defined by an integral elsewhere. It appears in probability distributions and volume formulas.

examples.explanation: At integers it recovers the factorial, shifted by one.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 5
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Beta function
definition: A two-argument special function closely tied to gamma: B(x,y) = Γ(x)Γ(y)/Γ(x+y). It normalizes the beta distribution in probability.

examples.explanation: Beta expressed through gamma.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 5
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Riemann zeta function
definition: Sums 1/nˢ over all positive integers. Its values at even integers involve powers of π; its zeros encode the distribution of primes, including the unproven Riemann hypothesis.

examples.explanation: The Basel problem: reciprocals of squares sum to π²/6.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 25
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Error function
definition: Captures areas under the bell curve: erf(x) is twice the normal area from 0 to x. Normal probabilities are arithmetic with erf.

examples.explanation: Scaled area under the Gaussian bell.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 7
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Bessel function
definition: Oscillating special functions solving radial wave problems: vibrations of drums, heat in cylinders, signal modes. J_n is the Bessel function of the first kind of order n.

examples.explanation: The zero-order Bessel function starts at 1 like cosine.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 10
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Group
definition: A set G with one operation satisfying closure, associativity, an identity element and inverses. Groups capture symmetry: rotations, permutations and number systems all form groups.

examples.explanation: Integers under addition: identity 0, inverse −n.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Isomorphism
definition: A structure-preserving correspondence between two objects: a bijection carrying the operations across. Isomorphic objects are algebraically the same, differing only in labels.

examples.explanation: The exponential maps addition to multiplication bijectively.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

notes: Shares the ≅ glyph with geometric congruence; the algebraic reading is set by context.

name: Modular congruence
definition: States that a and b leave the same remainder on division by n, equivalently n divides their difference. Congruence classes partition the integers into n residue systems.
reading: “a is congruent to b mod n”.

examples.explanation: Both leave remainder 5; their difference 12 is a multiple of 12.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 27
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Greatest common divisor
definition: The largest integer dividing both a and b. Euclid's algorithm computes it with repeated remainders; it underlies fraction reduction and modular inverses.
reading: “the g c d of a and b”.

examples.explanation: Six is the largest shared divisor.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Least common multiple
definition: The smallest positive integer that is a multiple of both a and b. It gives the least common denominator for adding fractions, and satisfies gcd(a,b)·lcm(a,b) = a·b.
reading: “the l c m of a and b”.

examples.explanation: Twelve is the first shared multiple.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Euler's totient function
definition: Counts integers from 1 to n that share no factor with n. It powers RSA cryptography via Euler's theorem: a^φ(n) ≡ 1 mod n for a coprime to n.

examples.explanation: 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 are coprime to 9.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 27
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Tensor product
definition: Builds a larger vector space from two smaller ones, with dimension multiplied. It combines quantum states, extends scalars, and writes the Kronecker product of matrices.

examples.explanation: Dimensions multiply under the tensor product.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Direct sum (exclusive or)
definition: In algebra, the direct sum combines structures component-wise. In logic and computing, the same glyph means exclusive or: exactly one side true.

examples.explanation: Dimensions add under direct sum.
Exactly one of P, Q holds.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

sources.license: Unicode License Agreement; glyph identity

name: Arg min and arg max
definition: Name where a minimum or maximum occurs, rather than its value. argmin f is the input achieving the smallest output; argmax the largest.

examples.explanation: The square is smallest at x = 3.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Fourier transform
definition: Decomposes a signal into its frequencies: the transform at each frequency measures how much of that oscillation the signal contains. It turns differentiation into multiplication and convolution into products.

examples.explanation: Correlate f against every oscillation frequency.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Laplace transform
definition: Converts differential equations into algebra by mapping functions of time to functions of a complex frequency s. Derivatives become multiplication by s, so circuits and controls solve with fractions.

examples.explanation: Differentiation becomes multiplication by s.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Big-O notation
definition: Bounds growth from above up to a constant factor: f is O(g) when |f| ≤ C·g eventually. It classifies algorithms (linear, quadratic, exponential) while ignoring hardware constants.

examples.explanation: Quadratic term dominates; constants and lower terms drop.
